chapter: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
title: Hearing Dizzy Gillespie with Cab Calloway on the radio
summary: Jones describes Dizzy picking notes like apples, and his debt to Roy Eldridge and earlier players.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: You mentioned having heard Dizzy with Cab Calloway on the radio.
And tell me what your reaction was when you heard him. You were telling me before, but it didn't get on the tape right.
Well, there was -- at that point Cab had a great outfit, really, you know?

He had some first class musicians. And guys like Chu Berry, who was a great tenor player. Jonah Jones. But this guy that was playing these different notes, Dizzy Gillespie, I didn't know who he was. I just heard him on the air. I said, 'Who in the heck is that? Who the hell is that playing? He's picking notes like a guy picking apples off of a tree.'
You know? Just reaching up there and just grabbing them, you know? And they were pretty, beautiful notes. And Dizzy, he was really hearing those things at that point. And he still does.

He's still a master, you know? Even though -- like I've said before, there are a lot of young good players now, but you can't -- you can't deny your predecessors. There's always somebody there to open the door and get the whole thing started. Now you can improve on it over a period of generations or expand it or whatever you might want to say, but you cannot ignore the first door that's been opened.
And Dizzy certainly acknowledges the doors that preceded him.
Yes. Back with Louis, Roy, Roy Eldridge, he -- I remember the time when Dizzy used to sound a lot like Roy Eldridge.
Well, he admits this. He said that Roy was his inspiration.
That he had to go through that to get where he was going.
Yeah. Roy was quite a man at one point, especially when he was with Gene Krupa, and as a soloist, oh,
boy, he was awfully powerful in those days.
